notes: Hook recomputed: it is a chosen example ("Say"), and its figures are the brief’s i8 worked case. A coil of 8 + j6 = 10∠36.87° Ω on 230 V draws 23∠−36.87° = 18.4 − j13.8 A; a −j10 Ω capacitor across it draws j23 A; the supply current is 18.4 + j9.2 A = 20.57 A, so "about 21 A" is right. 230 V is sourced (BBC Bitesize; UK Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations 2002, reg. 27), and the fall in supply current matches the power-factor sources (EEEGUIDE; Fiore, Engineering LibreTexts 7.3).

The hook only works because the coil has some resistance as well as reactance: a pure coil drawing 23 A would be cancelled completely by a capacitor drawing 23 A. That is consistent with the course (i7 makes impedance R + jX), so no change was needed.

In one breath checked against the research: × −1 is a 180° turn (Chemistry LibreTexts) and × j a +90° turn (Khan Academy), so j × j = −1 (mathcentre 7.1). Adding is vector addition (Sheffield 10.2). Multiplying multiplies the lengths and adds the angles (mathcentre 7.6). The form is chosen to suit the sum (Sheffield 10.2). Inductive impedance points up and capacitive impedance points down (ModEL). Impedance is in ohms and covers the whole opposition (OpenStax; Rose-Hulman). DC methods carry over with complex arithmetic (Utah; MIT 18.031). Nothing in it is overclaimed.
